transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-14
Start time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Grace (Redwood SE), Priya (CTO), Evan (SRE), Lena (ML Eng)

Auto-summary (auto): discussed tuning scheduler priority windows, token ceilings, continuous batching tradeoffs, and KV cache heuristics; agreed on benchmarks and action items.

00:00:00 - Aisha: okay folks, thanks for taking the time. we want to focus on throughput patterns and specific knobs - continous batching, priority windowing, and the token ceil. Marco will lead the tuning bits.
00:00:18 - Marco: hi all, quick agenda: first, show how our scheduler behaves at high concurrency, second, talk k v cache hit signals and how they affect packing, third, quantization caveats, then q&a.
00:00:33 - Priya: sounds good, we are mainly worried about p99 lat during bursts and keeping our onprem cluster under the egress limit.
00:00:42 - Evan: also want to avoid tail spikes — current baseline has p95 ~120ms but p99 jumps to 900ms when batch windows get long.
00:00:50 - Marco: yeah that's common — usually due to aggressive continuous batching and high max_num_seqs mixing small and large sequences.
00:01:05 - Grace: quick callout: our continuous_batching_enabled mode batches across tenants, so priority window and tenant affinity matter.
00:01:20 - Lena: can you clarify priority window? i've seen 'priority_window_ms' in docs but not sure its effect on packing.
00:01:30 - Marco: of course. priority_window_ms is the short wait period the scheduler holds a request to let higher priority small requests join the batch. it trades latency for packing efficiency. so increasing it raises average batching efficiency but may increase tail latency for initial requests. transcription note: word "k v" sometimes transcribed as 'k v'
00:01:50 - Aisha: and we also have a token_ceil mechanism? how does token_ceil interact with max_num_seqs?
00:01:58 - Marco: token_ceil is effectively a per-request token budget the scheduler won't exceed when packing. think of it as a guard against one huge request filling the batch and starving others. max_num_seqs is the max sequence count per batch on a GPU shard. so they together shape batch composition: token_ceil limits token-weighted packing, max_num_seqs caps the sequence count.
00:02:20 - Priya: our workload has a bimodal distribution — lots of short queries (~16 tokens) and occasional long context (~1,200 tokens) for document generation.
00:02:29 - Marco: that's classic problematic mix — continuous batching will happily pack the shorts together, but when a long arrives it can either be isolated or clog.
00:02:40 - Marco: recommended strategy: set token_ceil to something like 256 for general use, set max_num_seqs = 16 for our A100/80GB equivalent nodes, and tune priority_window_ms small e.g., 10-20ms to reduce p99. those numbers are starting points.
00:02:58 - Evan: if we set token_ceil 256, won't we lose throughput on the large generation jobs?
00:03:05 - Marco: you can have policy-based routing: route long jobs to dedicated pools (redwood dedicated) or to a fallback model variant with chunked generation. for onprem, we can reserve a node pool.
00:03:16 - Grace: also prefix KV cache helps a lot — if the long gen uses cached prefix keys, effective tokens compute as remaining tokens, so token_ceil behaves nicely. but the hit rate matters.
00:03:29 - Lena: what's the typical k v cache hit rate improvement we see after tuning?
00:03:34 - Marco: it depends; for chat-heavy workloads where prefixes repeat, we see KV hit increase from 30% to 70% after adding a small sticky affinity window and increasing cache retention from 90s to 300s. for document pipelines less re-use so smaller gains.
00:03:49 - Aisha: can you elaborate sticky affinity?
00:03:52 - Marco: sticky affinity pins requests from same session to same worker for a short grace period. that boosts local KV cache hit without global replication. in onprem that also helps because you control rack locality and can tune shard affinity.
00:04:05 - Priya: our security team wants no persistent cross-tenant cache replication, is sticky affinity ok?
00:04:11 - Grace: yes sticky affinity is local to the node and respects tenant boundaries; no cross-tenant keys are shared. for compliance we can provide the config that enforces it.
00:04:20 - Evan: what about quantization? we've experimented with int8 but saw slight quality drop on summarization. any guidance?
00:04:28 - Marco: quant is workload dependent — int8 usually safe for many models, but for summarization and instruction-following tasks small degradations can happen. options: use quant for short-token inference (embeddings or classification) but use fp16 or mixed for long-context generation. also use eval sets to check regression. note: transcription maybe 'quan' occasionally.
00:04:46 - Lena: could quantization affect k v cache layout or hit?
00:04:50 - Marco: not directly — k v cache is model-structure dependent. quant changes kernel speed and memory, which affects how many kv entries can live in GPU memory. smaller quant formats -> more kv entries -> higher effective hit potential because you can retain more history. tradeoff: evaluation risk.
00:05:05 - Priya: back to scheduler knobs: you suggested priority_window_ms 10-20ms. what about adaptive windows?
00:05:12 - Marco: we have an adaptive windowing option that shrinks the window during overload and grows it when idle. it's controlled by two thresholds: queue_util_high and queue_util_low and max_window_ms. it's more complex but can reduce p99 without losing too much throughput. costs: more config complexity and a need for good telemetry.
00:05:30 - Evan: do you have recommended metrics we should track during the pilot?
00:05:34 - Grace: yes - per-route p50/p95/p99 latencies, batch size distribution, kv cache hit rate, token-per-batch distribution, GPU utilization, and max_num_seqs throttled events. also track number of times token_ceil blocked composition (we expose this as token_ceil_count).
00:05:50 - Aisha: i'll include a dashboard template in the follow-up.
00:05:54 - Priya: VPC/onprem notes — our infra team requires that the control plane has minimal external egress and all keys via our KMS. do you support that?
00:06:03 - Marco: yes for Redwood Private we can run control plane connectors inside the VPC and integrate with customer KMS or HSM. there are options to run telemetry and logs to a customer S3 endpoint. some differences: autoscaler health checks need internal network access; we'll provide a hardened manifest for onprem.
00:06:20 - Evan: how about encrypted KV cache offload? we prefer not to store unencrypted snapshots on shared storage.
00:06:27 - Grace: we support encrypted checkpointing using customer keys; snapshots can be written to encrypted storage. we also support short TTLs for cache persistence if you want to avoid local disk retention.
00:06:39 - Priya: great, can we talk about an extreme case: high burst of 10k concurrent small requests for search followed by a few long gens. what's the tuning?
00:06:49 - Marco: for that pattern, two-pool approach works well: a search-optimized pool with small token_ceil (e.g., 64), small max_num_seqs high count like 32 but small window, and a generation pool with larger token_ceil and fewer seqs. fast routing (policy) based on route metadata (api key or path) routes to the right pool. if you can't split, then tune priority windows very small and use early rejection fallback to a cheaper model for long gens.
00:07:13 - Lena: is there a way to detect 'long' requests early and preempt packing?
00:07:17 - Marco: yes we expose an early-size header where SDKs can indicate expected tokens_remaining. the scheduler uses it to treat those as 'heavy' and put them into a separate queue or mark them with lower packing priority. this saves packing disruptions.
00:07:30 - Evan: SDK change needed?
00:07:32 - Marco: minimal, we support it in our Python and Node SDKs; header is x-expected-tokens.
00:07:38 - Aisha: quick interjection — there's some noise, sorry —
00:07:44 - Priya: no worries. some of this is new to our infra folks. any recommendations for the first pilot config?
00:07:50 - Marco: start with: continuous_batching_enabled=true, priority_window_ms=15, token_ceil=256, max_num_seqs=16, sticky_affinity_ttl=120s, kv_cache_retention=300s. run two 2-hour benchmarks: one steady load, one peaky bursts. capture the metrics Grace mentioned.
00:08:08 - Priya: ok that seems reasonable.
00:08:11 - Marco: also watch for token ceiling events — we log token_ceil_count per route. if you see many events, either raise token_ceil or route heavy flows elsewhere.
00:08:22 - Evan: how do we measure warm vs cold cache impact on latency?
00:08:26 - Grace: run a warmstart test: preload common prefixes and measure latency delta; we usually run a cold-start sweep that evicts caches then replay baseline traffic. the delta shows impact. additionally, look at kv_cache_hitrate over time.
00:08:39 - Lena: what about quantization + scheduler: do we need different max_num_seqs when using int8?
00:08:44 - Marco: yes int8 reduces memory per token so you might bump max_num_seqs up by 1.2-1.5x. however kernel throughput characteristics might differ so benchmark for p99 not just throughput. sometimes increasing seqs raises p99.
00:08:58 - Priya: any pitfalls on onprem GPUs? we've got mixed smaller T4s and a few A100s.
00:09:05 - Marco: mixed GPU pools complicate universal packing. best to partition by GPU capability and set shard affinity rules. for T4s use smaller max_num_seqs and smaller window. or route different model quant flavors to different GPU types.
00:09:20 - Evan: will Redwood console show per-node batch distributions for onprem?
00:09:24 - Grace: yes; console (or a local dashboard for Private) exposes per-node batch sizes, token distributions, and shard affinity. for Private we can also ship prometheus exporters.
00:09:35 - Aisha: let's open the floor for detailed q's — Priya?
00:09:39 - Priya: is there a recommended threshold for queue_util_high when using adaptive windowing?
00:09:44 - Marco: we typically start with queue_util_high=0.75 and queue_util_low=0.35, max_window_ms=50. tune based on observed p99 vs throughput tradeoffs.
00:09:56 - Lena: any automatic fallback when GPU saturation causes contention?
00:09:59 - Marco: yes built-in fallbacks: model-variant fallback to cheaper quantized model, or degrade to a lower-latency shorter-context mode. we also have cross-region fallback if capacity constrained in a region but that is more for hosted. onprem you can configure local fallback policies.
00:10:16 - Evan: curious — does token_ceil affect billing metering?
00:10:19 - Aisha: good question, usage accounting measures actual tokens executed. token_ceil only affects packing, not billable token counts. if you route heavy jobs to dedicated pool it might affect contract usage.
00:10:30 - Priya: what about throttling? we have strict SLA with internal product teams, need backpressure signals.
00:10:35 - Marco: we emit backpressure metrics and we support token-based admission control. also you can set per-api-key qps and token quotas.
00:10:44 - Lena: any notes about data residency for snapshots or KV persists?
00:10:48 - Grace: onprem snapshots are written to customer-provided storage; for cloud Hosted we support region-restricted storage. customer keys are supported via KMS integrations.
00:10:58 - Evan: fine. last question — how much effort to change max_num_seqs at runtime?
00:11:03 - Marco: it's a hot-reload knob. you can change per-pool via the control plane and workers will pick up within 30-60 seconds without restart. however bumping it too high can cause memory pressure so monitor GPU memory free.
00:11:15 - Priya: okay good.
00:11:18 - Aisha: summary — we agreed to run pilot with the config Marco suggested, Marco+Grace will run the benchmarks, Lena will provide request distribution, Evan will validate firewall/KMS constraints, Aisha will share dashboards and config templates.
00:11:33 - Marco: i'll also include example prometheus queries for token_ceil_count, kv_cache_hitrate, and batch_size_histogram.
00:11:39 - Priya: thanks everyone, this was very helpful.
00:11:43 - Aisha: end notes: i'll follow-up in email with links to the config repo, the security packet, and the scheduling playbook.
00:11:51 - (meeting ends)
